lead: Both readings are about the one God whose love reaches beyond every boundary. Paul tells the Corinthians that knowledge puffs up but love builds up, and gives them one of the earliest Christian confessions: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. In Mark, a Gentile mother from the region of Tyre asks Jesus to heal her daughter, and her humble, quick-witted faith wins the healing. The one Lord is Lord of all, and humble love opens the way to him.

r.h: One God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ
set: The Corinthians had written to Paul with questions (7:1), and here he turns to a practical one: may Christians eat meat that had been offered to idols? In a Greek city much of the meat sold in the market came from temple sacrifices, and meals with friends were often held in temple dining halls. Some Corinthians said, “We know that idols are nothing, so we may eat anything.” Paul agrees with the truth they know, but he corrects the pride with which they hold it. Chapters 8 to 10 treat the question; today’s verses lay the foundation.
str: vv. 1–3: knowledge puffs up, love builds up; whoever loves God is known by him.
v. 4: no idol really exists; there is no God but one.
v. 5: there are so-called gods and lords.
v. 6: the confession: one God, the Father, from whom are all things; one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.
kw: The Corinthians prized spiritual knowledge. Paul does not despise it, but knowledge without love makes a person proud and careless of others.
Literally “build a house”. Love builds the community like a house; Paul uses the word often in these chapters (8:10; 10:23; 14:4).

Paul takes the Shema, “The Lord is our God, the Lord alone” (Deuteronomy 6:4), and unfolds it: “God” is said of the Father, “Lord” of Jesus Christ. Jesus is placed within the confession of the one God of Israel.
vv: Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
A short sentence that judges much clever religion. Truth must be spoken and held in love (see 13:2).
but anyone who loves God is known by him.
Paul turns the question around. What matters most is not what we know about God but that God knows us, and to be known by God is to be loved by him.
yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.

Little more than twenty years after the Resurrection, Paul speaks of Jesus as the one through whom all things were made, the work of God alone. This verse is a seed of the Creed: “one Lord Jesus Christ… through him all things were made.”
ch: The Catechism quotes the Second Council of Constantinople, which draws on this verse: “one God and Father from whom all things are, one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things are, and one Holy Spirit in whom all things are” (CCC 258). The whole Trinity works as one in creation and salvation, each Person according to what is proper to him. On the question that follows, the Catechism quotes Paul’s warning about wounding a brother’s weak conscience, by which one sins against Christ (CCC 1789, citing 8:12): love for the neighbour’s conscience must guide how we use our freedom.

r.h: Even the dogs under the table
set: Jesus has just taught that what makes a person unclean comes from the heart, not from food (7:14–23). Now he goes into Gentile territory, the region of Tyre on the Phoenician coast, north of Galilee. He wants to stay hidden, perhaps to rest with his disciples. There a Gentile woman comes to him. Mark calls her a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth: a woman of another people and religion.

The story is told after a meal of five thousand where twelve baskets of bread were left over (6:43) and before the feeding of four thousand in a Gentile area (8:1–9). Bread runs through these chapters.
str: v. 24: Jesus goes to Tyre and wants no one to know.
vv. 25–26: a Gentile woman falls at his feet and begs him to deliver her daughter.
v. 27: the hard answer: let the children be fed first.
v. 28: her reply: even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.
vv. 29–30: for that word her daughter is delivered; she goes home and finds the child well.
kw: Mark gives both her language and culture (Greek) and her birth (Phoenician of Syria). She is wholly outside Israel.
The diminutive suggests house dogs, not street dogs. Jesus’ words still sound hard. Many commentators see him testing and drawing out her faith; she takes up his own image and turns it into a plea.
“Let the children be fed first.” The word leaves the door open: Israel first, then the nations. Paul says the same: the Gospel is “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).
vv: Let the children be fed first, for it is not fair to take the children’s food and throw it to the dogs.
Jesus’ mission was first to Israel, God’s children by covenant. His word is not a refusal of the woman but a statement of order in God’s plan.
But she answered him, “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.”
She is the only person in Mark who wins an argument with Jesus. She does not deny Israel’s place; she asks only for a crumb, sure that a crumb of his power is enough.
So she went home, found the child lying on the bed, and the demon gone.
Jesus heals from a distance, without seeing the child. The mother believed his word and went home; she found it true.
ch: The Church sees in this woman a model of humble and persevering prayer. St Augustine, preaching on Matthew’s account of the same woman, praises her humility: she did not take offence at being compared to a dog, but accepted it and so was raised up (in substance, Sermon 77). The story also shows the Gospel going out to all peoples, as the Lord willed: the crumbs from Israel’s table become the bread of the nations, and the Church is sent to all (CCC 849).

qa: Was Jesus being harsh or prejudiced toward the woman?

Jesus’ words do sound hard, and the Gospel does not soften them. But the whole story shows his purpose: he does heal her daughter, and he praises her answer. He tests her faith and lets it shine. He came first to Israel, as God had planned, and through Israel to all nations. The woman understood that, and believed that there was enough for her too.
study: Paul says knowledge puffs up but love builds up. When I share what I know about the faith, does it build others up?
The Syrophoenician mother would not give up. For whom am I praying with that kind of humble persistence?
